articles.title: Two npm Bugs, One Lesson: Upgrading the Runtime Is Not Upgrading the Dependencies
articles.excerpt: Two npm Bugs, One Lesson: Upgrading the Runtime Is Not Upgrading the Dependencies Two advisories published this month describe failures in ordinary libraries. One is a JWT verification bug that turns…
articles.body: Two npm Bugs, One Lesson: Upgrading the Runtime Is Not Upgrading the Dependencies Two advisories published this month describe failures in ordinary libraries. One is a JWT verification bug that turns a public key into a shared secret. The other is a path traversal that walks out of a target directory through a symlink chain. At the code level they share nothing; operationally they are the same problem, because both are fixed by a dependency bump and neither is fixed by upgrading the runtime. fast-jwt: when a public key becomes a shared secret CVE-2026-107722, CVSS 9.8, affects npm package fast-jwt versions 6.2.0 through 6.3.0. The mechanism deserves attention because the fix is a version number while the failure is a parsing assumption.

articles.title: How to Humanize AI Text in Python: A Linter for Robotic Phrases + the Top 5 Free Tools (2026)
articles.excerpt: Updated October 2026. I'm on the team behind UnAIMyText, which is #3 below. Code is MIT-style: copy it freely. If you generate text with an LLM in a script, whether product descriptions, changelogs or…
articles.body: Updated October 2026. I'm on the team behind UnAIMyText, which is #3 below. Code is MIT-style: copy it freely. If you generate text with an LLM in a script, whether product descriptions, changelogs or support replies, you've probably seen the same tics come back: "Moreover," "It is important to note," "delve," "in today's fast-paced world." You can't fix them with taste at scale, but you can lint for them the way you lint code. This post builds a tiny Python checker that flags robotic phrasing, then covers five free tools for the rewrite step. The goal is clearer, more natural prose, not tricking anyone. Step 1: build a phrase linter Python's re module is enough. We'll flag three things: stock filler phrases, sentence-length monotony and repeated sentence openers.

articles.title: Your Agent Is a Guest: Egress Policy for Agent Fleets
articles.excerpt: Most agent code I review is careful about what it does inside the sandbox and careless about what it does on the way out. Then it hits a site that returns 403 to anything with python-httpx in the User…
articles.body: Most agent code I review is careful about what it does inside the sandbox and careless about what it does on the way out. Then it hits a site that returns 403 to anything with python-httpx in the User-Agent, retries forty times, and burns an afternoon. The web is getting less tolerant of agents. Publishers are blocking crawlers outright, CDNs fingerprint TLS and headers, and more sites are moving to "pay for the API or go away." That's not a temporary mood — it's the steady state. If your fleet fetches anything from a domain you don't own, egress is a subsystem you have to design, not a client.get() call you sprinkle through a tool. This is the view from the proxy layer: what breaks, what to log, and what to put in front of the agents.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.body: The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore.
